sections.normalized_html: Let [MATH: A(-1,4, -5)] and [MATH: B(2,3,5)]. Find [MATH: \overrightarrow{AB}] in column vector notation.
sections.readable_text: Let [MATH: A(-1,4, -5)] and [MATH: B(2,3,5)]. Find [MATH: \overrightarrow{AB}] in column vector notation.

sections.normalized_html:
We have

[MATH: OA^(→) = a = − i + 4j − 5k,; OB^(→) = b = 2i + 3j + 5k.]

Now, we can express [MATH: \overrightarrow{AB}] as the difference of position vectors, as follows:

[MATH: AB^(→)|= b − a; = (2i + 3j + 5k) − (− i + 4j − 5k); = 3i − j + 10k; = [3; − 1; 10]]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can use Cartesian coordinates to define vectors in three-dimensional space. For example, consider a point [MATH: A(2,2,3),] and define the origin as the point [MATH: O(0,0,0).] The position vector of [MATH: A] is [MATH: \overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}.]

Content:
Let's also define three special unit vectors [MATH: \mathbf{i},] [MATH: \mathbf{j},] and [MATH: \mathbf{k},] where [MATH: |\,\mathbf{i}\,| = |\,\mathbf{j}\,| = |\,\mathbf{k}\,| = 1,] as follows:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{i}] is a horizontal unit vector that points "outwards" along the positive direction of the [MATH: x]-axis,
- [MATH: \mathbf{j}] is a horizontal unit vector that points to the right along the positive direction of the [MATH: y]-axis, and
- [MATH: \mathbf{k}] is a vertical unit vector that points upwards along the positive direction of the [MATH: z]-axis.

Content:
All of these vectors are illustrated in the diagram shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/777665cba0031bbdfc2ad08e4a6504ae]

Content:
Now, we can uniquely describe our position vector using [MATH: \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}] as
[MATH: a|= OA^(→) = 2i + 2j + 3k.]

---
